Comment 1.1.response: The reviewer is right that nothing in the objective forces the map to behave like a confidence, and the submitted paper should not have called it calibrated. We now test the claim directly rather than assert it. Section V H compares the map against the absolute error of the backbone output with respect to the clean reference on every test image. The quantity tested is the demand map $u = 1 - c$, the one the wrapper acts on, and two diagnostics are reported, the rank correlation and the sparsification error. The answer is that the map does not carry the meaning the submitted paper claimed. The pooled rank correlation between the map and the backbone error over the 173 test images is minus 0.258, so the map is not merely uninformative but ordered the wrong way. The sparsification test agrees. Removing the pixels the map ranks as least reliable raises the remaining error to 1.88 times its starting value, against an oracle ranking that reaches 0.07, so the sparsification error is 0.776. We do not report an expected calibration error, since the map is not a probability and no calibration target is defined for it. The component is renamed a learned cooperation map throughout the paper, the word calibrated is not used of the map anywhere, and Section V H states that the map predicts where a correction helps rather than how wrong the backbone is. The map is nevertheless contributing measurably to the result. Replacing it by a constant lowers the contrast gain from plus 3.71 to plus 2.51 percent and worsens five of the six clinical measures, which is why we kept it and renamed it rather than removing it. The cooperation term in Section V A is the only place the map is trained toward a meaning. It rewards agreement between the map and the estimated correction potential, so the map is pushed to be high where the correction has room to act. Whether that coincides with backbone error is exactly what Section V H measures.
changes: Section V H is new.
The map is renamed a learned cooperation map in Section III A and everywhere else it appears, and the word calibrated is removed from the paper.

Comment 1.2.response: We added the study the reviewer asked for. Section V F removes one property at a time at test time, which sets its score to the satisfied value and its failure map to zero, and re evaluates the whole 173 image test set with the reported NAFNet model. Panel (a) of Fig. S1 of the supplementary file draws the result as a heat map, one row per property removed and one column per measure, with the value printed in every cell. The honest summary is that the six properties are not equally important. The costliest single removal is the speckle conformity property P5, which takes 3.19 points of the equivalent number of looks gain, 1.28 points of boundary sharpness and 0.94 points of the tissue contrast index. Removing the edge continuity property P1 costs 1.72 points of the speckle gain and 0.45 points of the signal to noise gain. Removing the local contrast property P2 costs 0.74 points of the speckle gain and leaves contrast unchanged, at plus 0.12 points. Removing P3 or P6 changes no measure by more than 0.23 points, on the speckle gain for $P_6$, and removing P4 changes no measure by more than 0.04 points. All numbers above were recomputed on the selected checkpoint, the seed 0 model of the tissue bounded gate setting at dead zone 0.6, which is the seed 0 checkpoint Table 5 studies, while Table 3 reports the mean over three seeds. The six failure maps themselves are now Fig. 2 of the main paper, moved in from the supplementary file so a reader can see what each property is looking at before reading what removing it costs. The earlier version of this study had been run on a different checkpoint, and we corrected that before quoting it. We have kept all six rather than pruning the three that are close to inert, for a reason we state in the paper. The properties are the vocabulary of the rule layer and of the explanation shown to the reader, and a property that rarely changes the output on this test set can still be the one that fires on a different scanner or a pathological scan. But we say plainly that on PKU37 three of the six carry almost all of the effect. We stop short of saying that P3, P4 and P6 can be dropped together, since each number above comes from removing one property on its own and we did not measure the three removed at once.
changes: Section V F is new, and Fig. S1 of the supplementary file.
The full leave one out table is in the supplementary file, generated as tab_lopo.tex.
Section VI B, Limitations, states that half the property set is close to inert on this test set.

Comment 1.3.response: We agree that this is the right question to ask of any method that raises contrast, and the submitted paper did not answer it. Section V J is new and measures the risk directly, using the clean reference that PKU37 provides. Four quantities are reported over the whole test set. The rate at which an edge appears in the corrected image where the reference has none, before and after correction. The rate rises, from 0.45 percent of pixels for the backbone output to 0.48 percent after correction, an increase on 127 of the 173 images. We report this as a cost rather than presenting it as a null result. The retention of weak structures, defined as structures whose contrast in the reference lies in the lowest decile, before and after correction. Retention falls, from 40.5 percent to 37.6 percent, on 168 of the 173 images. This is the clearest cost of the method on this test set and we state it in the results and in the limitations. The behavior inside dark fluid like regions enclosed by tissue, reported as the fraction of the image they occupy and the mean absolute change inside them. Dark regions occupy 1.6 percent of the image area and the mean absolute change inside them is 0.0022, against 0.0067 over the whole image, so the correction is about three times quieter where a hypodense region carries the finding. The largest change on any single image across the test set, and the shift of the two strongest layer boundaries. The mean absolute change over the whole image is 0.0067 and the largest change on any single image is 0.0178. The mean absolute shift of the inner limiting membrane goes from 4.73 to 4.38 pixels and of the retinal pigment epithelium from 9.93 to 10.03 pixels, so the first improves and the second is unchanged within the spread across images. Both happened, and we have done exactly that. The first sentence of Section V J now states that the correction raises the invented edge rate and lowers weak structure retention, both by small but significant amounts, and the limitations name both. We did not soften either, and we did not reselect the model to avoid them, because the selection criterion was fixed on the validation split before the test set was scored. One structural fact bounds the risk. The gate suppresses change in the dark region, so a boundary can only be moved by the additive edge branch within that cap. Section VI B states plainly that no clinician read these images and that a reader study is the correct next step. We also asked whether the criterion that selected the operating point is blind to these two measures, since it scores six clinical measures and fidelity and neither of the safety measures. It is. Measured on the validation split, so that the test split is used once, the setting the criterion ranked second for NAFNet raises weak structure retention from 40.7 to 43.9 percent where the selected setting lowers it to 37.7, and adds less to the invented edge rate. We report this in the limitations and we did not reselect on it, because the criterion was fixed before the test split was scored and changing it afterwards would spend that split twice.
changes: Section V J is new.
Fig. S1 of the supplementary file draws the safety quantities.
Section VI B states that no expert reading was performed.
Section VI B states both regressions and reports the validation measurement of what the selection criterion does not see.

Comment 1.4.response: The reviewer's question is what led us to the defect described at the start of this letter, and we answer it in three parts. What the constants were. The weights 1.5 and 2.0 in the submitted paper were the initial values of learnable parameters that never moved, because the rule layer was saturated and received no gradient. They were not chosen at all. What they are now. Section III C states the allocation rule in full. The five budgets are fixed by one identity, that the base ceiling plus the positive budgets equals one and the base floor minus the negative budgets equals zero, which keeps the allocation inside the unit interval without clipping and lets the rule weights train. The rule weights themselves are learned, and Section V B says which quantities were selected on validation. Only one is, the fidelity dead zone, together with the choice of background rule. Whether any of it materially affects the result. Section V F varies the base level, the two rule weights that carry the allocation, and the conjunction, and re evaluates, with the budgets held fixed throughout by the identity above. Across the fourteen variations no measure turns negative. The largest change in any clinical measure is 0.77 points, on contrast, produced by moving the base level to its lowest setting. The budgets are tied by the identity that keeps the allocation inside the unit interval, so they are held fixed and we vary the base level and the two rule weights that carry the allocation, each of which moves the result by less than 0.2 points. Replacing the Lukasiewicz conjunction by the product moves contrast from plus 3.71 to plus 3.54 percent and by the minimum to plus 3.47 percent, with the other five measures within one part in fifty, so the two alternatives do differ but only slightly. We take the first branch and state both sides of it. One constant matters, the base allocation level, and lowering it trades fidelity for contrast in the direction the design predicts. Everything else, including the choice of conjunction, moves the result very little. We say in the paper that this means the result rests on the shape of the rule layer rather than on the particular logic, which is a reassurance about robustness and a limitation on how much the specific fuzzy calculus can be claimed to contribute.
changes: Section III C states the allocation rule and the identity that fixes its budgets.
Section V B states what was selected and how.
Section V F is the sensitivity study, and Fig. S1 of the supplementary file.

Comment 1.5.response: We agree and we have expanded both the review and the discussion. The related work is now Section I C, and its third part, on symbolic reasoning and expert networks joined with neural networks, is new. It covers three strands. The first is neuro symbolic work in medical imaging, including report generation that pairs a generative network with a symbolic knowledge graph, a probabilistic logic program layered on a convolutional feature extractor, and a knowledge graph attached to a learned model for corneal topography. The second is fuzzy rule systems embedded inside networks, including rough fuzzy discretization inside a network that processes OCT directly, and pixel level fuzzy rules used in place of a learned attention block. The third is expert network work, including steered mixtures of experts for denoising, its application to OCT speckle, and restoration networks that route an input through experts of different capacity. Thirteen works are now cited and discussed in that subsection, ten of them added in this revision. Section I C positions our method against them and Section VI B says what the correction layer buys. The common principle is that a learned component becomes easier to trust when part of the decision is written in a language a person can read. What is missing in that literature is a rule layer that acts on the output of a strong denoiser, names the clinical properties it protects, and limits how far it may move the image.
changes: Section I C is new.
Eleven references added.
Section VI B positions the method against that literature.

Comment 1.6.response: Thank you. The manuscript and the supplementary file have been revised for grammar, terminology, notation and sentence clarity rather than proof read in place. We also checked the section references, the figure captions and the tables against the built documents, so every pointer resolves to the place it names. The words experiment and experimental have been removed throughout, which is Reviewer 3 comment 15.

Every section, table, figure and equation reference was checked against the built documents.
The words experiment and experimental do not appear in either document.

Comment 2.1.response: The reviewer is right, and the two descriptions in the submitted paper were not consistent. We investigated and the implementation audit settled it. The submitted cross dataset numbers were produced by a script that resumes from the corrector trained on PKU37 and then fine tunes it for fifteen epochs on the other images of the target dataset in every fold, with elastic weight consolidation and with the backbone frozen except for the confidence head. That is few shot adaptation on the target scanner. It is not the transfer without training that the text claimed. We corrected this in the strongest way available, which is to make the honest protocol the primary one. Section V C, under the heading Transfer protocol, states the protocol exactly. Table 4 reports the model trained once on PKU37 and applied directly to Duke17 and Duke2013, with no parameter updated, no threshold recalibrated, and no statistic of the target images used to select anything. The only per image quantity is the background gate, which is part of the method and is computed identically on PKU37. The selected NAFNet setting does use the tissue bounded gate, so that sentence was changed. It now says that no Duke statistic is used to select anything beyond the per image quantity the gate itself computes, by the same rule already applied on PKU37, which is true of both members of the gate family. Section V B names the gate selected for each backbone. The revision also splits the single merged table of the first revision into three. Table 3 is the test set, Table 4 the transfer with nothing refitted, and Table 5 the component removals and the alternative operators. Table 4 gives the mean over three seeds for all four backbones on both target sets, with the seed spread in the fidelity column and encoded as bold in the clinical columns, and Table S6 of the supplementary file restores the spread of every clinical cell. Of those 48 backbone by measure by set pairs 40 are positive, with contrast rising in every one of the eight rows. The adapted protocol is reported only in Table S7 of the supplementary file. Each of its folds keeps the epoch that scores best on the subject it then reports, so those numbers are selected on the data they describe. We label them a historical diagnostic and do not use them to argue what adaptation achieves.
changes: Section V C, under the heading Transfer protocol, is new.
Table 4 is the frozen transfer and Table S7 of the supplementary file is the adapted protocol, kept as a historical diagnostic.
Both protocols have a driver in the release, scripts/eval_transfer.sh and scripts/eval_transfer_adapted.sh.

Comment 2.2.response: Section VI A is new and explains the trade off and when it is worth accepting. A denoiser trained on squared error already sits near a local optimum of that error, so a change that raises contrast or boundary definition generally moves away from it. We now report this as an observed average rather than a rule. Fidelity falls in the mean on all four backbones, from 0.17 dB on SwinIR to 0.98 dB on DnCNN, and it does not fall on every image, since the NAFNet panel of Fig. 3 gains 0.02 dB while its contrast rises. What we claim is the trade the means describe, an average cost under one decibel against gains in the quantities a grader uses to place a boundary or judge a fluid pocket. We have removed the comparison with the variation between two acquisitions of the same eye, since we did not measure that variation on this data and should not have asserted it. On the transformer backbone we owe the reviewer a correction as well as an explanation. Part of the SwinIR drop in the submitted version was ours. That corrector had been trained against a half resolution cache of the backbone output and then tested against the full resolution output, and the two references differ by 1.61 dB. The cache now runs at full resolution. The revised SwinIR number is therefore not comparable with the submitted one, and the discussion in Section VI A explains the remaining drop by the windowed attention, which smooths aggressively inside a window and so gives away the most contrast for the correction to restore. We withdraw what the submitted letter said about controlling this through the safety layer. The acceptance rule is a majority test and guarantees neither fidelity nor any individual condition. Tightening one of the three constraints need not change the output at all, since the candidate is accepted in full whenever the other two hold. A deployment that must lose less fidelity should lower the gain bound, which attenuates the multiplicative branch, though we cannot claim that monotonically improves fidelity, because the additive edge branch and the background operation stay active. Only bypassing the wrapper reproduces the backbone output exactly. The dead zone of the fidelity term is the training time counterpart, and Section V B reports how the result moves with it.
changes: Section VI A is new.
The SwinIR reference mismatch is stated and corrected, see the opening of this letter.
Section V B reports the dead zone as the one tuned fidelity budget.

Comment 3.1.response: The introduction has been rebuilt. Section I B now gives a numbered list of four new ideas, each with a pointer to the section that delivers it. They are six clinical properties in closed form that need no clean image at test time, a rule layer whose decision cannot jump, with the bound proved and then measured, a safety layer that decides how much of a proposal to keep, and one design carried across four denoisers. The list also says what is not new. Edge filters, cooperation maps and fuzzy operators are not claimed as contributions on their own.
changes: Section I B is new.

Comment 3.2.response: Section I A now argues the motivation from the clinical problem downward. The gap is not a missing denoiser, since strong denoisers already exist. It is the absence of anything between the denoiser and the reader that states what a good OCT image should look like and repairs the specific ways a denoised image falls short. We also say why building that missing part as another neural block would reproduce the original problem, because the reason for every change would again be hidden in learned weights.
changes: Section I A rewritten.

Comment 3.3.response: All three works are now cited and discussed where they are relevant rather than listed. The evolving fuzzy model work is cited in the subsection on fuzzy and expert systems as an example of identifying model structure from data. The model and data driven reconstruction work is cited as an example of combining a learned component with a physical forward operator. The work on the sensitivity of a differential model to its initial values is cited in the same paragraph as an example of studying how a model responds to perturbation of its inputs, which is the same question our stability analysis asks of the rule layer. The bibliography gives volume, issue, pages and year for every entry and no digital object identifiers, which is the style used throughout. We were unable to verify a digital object identifier for the first of the three on the publisher pages we could reach, so that entry is given with its volume, issue, pages and year and without a digital object identifier. We will add it if the editorial office can supply it.
changes: Three references added and discussed in Section I C.

Comment 3.4.response: This was a fair criticism, because the submitted paper used the word without defining it. Section III C now gives Definition 1 before the theorem and says what the word does not mean here. It is not stability in the sense of Lyapunov and we claim no fixed point. The definition, Equation 5, is Lipschitz stability of the allocation with respect to the vector of the five rule truth values in the maximum norm, and its constant is Equation 6. A small change in the evidence produces a proportionally small change in the decision, and the constant is the worst case ratio between the two. We chose that notion because the rule truth values are exactly what shift when the backbone is replaced or the scanner changes, so bounding the response to them is the property that matters for the transfer claim. Section V I then measures the realized ratio on real images against the constant.
changes: Section III C, Definition 1 and Equations 5 and 6.
Section V I measures the constant, see the response to comment 3.12.

Comment 3.5.response: Section II B is new and states the problem in the standard form. The decision variables are the wrapper parameters, with the backbone parameters held fixed. The objective is the expectation over paired data of a weighted sum of six terms, Equation 1, each of which is defined in Section V A. The three constraints are stated and then given formally in Section IV B. The problem is solved by mini batch stochastic gradient descent with AdamW, which is possible because every logical connective is replaced by a smooth piecewise linear surrogate. The reviewer notes that optimization could be well linked to learning, and we have made that link explicit, including one place where the submitted description was wrong. The three acceptance conditions are not relaxed into the objective and no penalty stands in for them. They are evaluated exactly, per image, at test time only, where the number that hold sets the blend weight. Training therefore optimizes the candidate and not the blended output, since the acceptance rule does not run while the wrapper is fitted. The regularization the objective does carry is Equation 19, which bounds the size and roughness of the change and protects the background, and is a separate thing from the three conditions.
changes: Section II B is new.

Comment 3.6.response: We agree that the notation was dense. Section II A is new and fixes it. Every symbol is now defined in words at its first use. Table 1 collects the symbols that recur across sections, in the order in which the paper introduces them, and a symbol used in one place only is defined in the sentence that introduces it. Nested subscripts have been removed. Quantities that were written with a descriptive subscript inside a hat are now single letters. As one example, the corrected candidate is now simply q.
changes: Section II A and Table 1.
Nested and descriptive subscripts replaced by single letters throughout.

Comment 3.9.response: Two things were asked, a justification of each property and a sensitivity study. Both are now in the paper. Justification. Table 2 gives, for each of the six properties, the clinical failure it names, its aggregate score and its failure map in closed form, where the map is large, and its threshold. The named subterms are expanded in Section S1 of the supplementary file, which is the one pointer the property definitions still make. The scores are all computed from the noisy input and the backbone output alone and each is written as a formula so it can be recomputed from the release. The mathematical reason for the form of each is given in the text of Section III B. Sensitivity. Section V F and Section V F.

Comment 3.10.response: The training account is new and is now the first part of Section V, which holds the training, the tests and the results together. Section V B answers the question about paired data directly, because we agree it was not clear. Training uses paired data. The clean reference enters the fidelity term and the clinical term and it supervises the additive edge branch. Nothing in the method is unsupervised. Testing uses no clean image at any point. The six clinical properties are computed from the noisy input and the backbone output alone, which is what ground truth free means in this paper. It refers to the inputs of the rule layer at test time and not to the training procedure. Section V A gives the six loss terms as Equations 14 to 19 with what each measures and why that form was chosen. Preparing this revision we read the objective of the submitted paper against the training code and found three mismatches. The clinical term is a weighted one sided penalty against a target taken from the backbone and not a sum of log ratios, it runs over nine quantities and not two, the edge term is weighted toward the clean edges and carries two further parts, and a sixth term of bounds and background protection was missing from the objective altogether. All three are corrected, with every weight and constant printed. Section V B gives the schedule, the two stages, the optimizer and the three learning rates, and Algorithm 1 of the supplementary file states the procedure step by step. The seed, the dead zone and the frozen normalization statistics are given in the text around it rather than as inputs of the algorithm itself. The same subsection states how the operating point was chosen, gives the initialization, and lists every constant with its origin, marked fixed, measured, selected or learned. We also record the exact training command in the release, because we found while preparing this revision that the command used for the submitted results had not been recorded. Every number in the revised paper comes from a checkpoint produced by that recorded script, selected on validation by a recorded rule, and scored on test without retraining.
changes: Section V is new Paired data, loss terms, schedule, operating point, and initialization with every constant and its origin.
Algorithm 1 of the supplementary file, file supp/sections/S3_training.
The training and selection scripts are in the release, scripts/train_all.sh and scripts/select_config.sh.

Comment 3.11.response: We have added a quantitative safety study and we state plainly what it does not cover. Section V J measures invented edges against the clean reference, retention of weak structures, the change inside dark fluid like regions enclosed by tissue, and the largest change on any single image. The response to Reviewer 1 comment 3 lists the quantities. The invented edge rate rises from 0.45 to 0.48 percent of pixels, weak structure retention falls from 40.5 to 37.6 percent, dark regions occupy 1.6 percent of the area with a mean absolute change of 0.0022 inside them against 0.0067 over the whole image, the inner limiting membrane shift improves from 4.73 to 4.38 pixels, the retinal pigment epithelium shift is 9.93 against 10.03 pixels, and boundary sharpness is not worsened on 104 of the 173 images. The first two are costs and we report them as such. On lesions and expert assessment we have to be direct. PKU37, Duke17 and Duke2013 are denoising datasets and carry no lesion annotation, and no clinician read the outputs of this method. The dark region analysis is our proxy for fluid, and the weak structure analysis is our proxy for thin layers and subtle features, and we say in Section V J and in Section VI B that they are proxies. A reader study on annotated pathology is the correct next step and is outside the scope of this revision.
changes: Section V J is new.
Section VI B, Limitations, states that no expert reading was performed and that the safety study uses proxies.

Comment 3.12.response: Section V I is new and tests both theoretical claims numerically on the test set, and Section I B, Section III C and Section IV C each now point forward to it. Three things are checked. For the stability result, Theorem 1, we perturb the rule truth values by a controlled amount and measure the ratio of Definition 1, then compare it with the constant of Equation 6 computed from the trained weights. The constant is 0.5489 and the largest ratio measured over the 173 test images is 0.4679. The constant is exact for the allocation as a function of the rule truth values, so the gap is not slack in the proof. It means the perturbations a real image produces never reach the worst case the constant allows. For the contrast result, Theorem 2, we measure the tissue gain, the background leakage and the ratio of background standard deviations on every image and report on how many images the hypotheses hold. The margin condition holds on 139 of the 173 images and the standard deviation ratio condition on 94, a bare majority, with mean ratio 0.976. The two leakage terms have means of minus 0.0007 in tissue and minus 0.0017 in background against a mean absolute change of 0.0067 over the whole image. Their means sit near zero with a long negative tail, so we also report the per image sign, which is what the margin condition depends on. The tissue term is positive on 137 images and the background term negative on 107. Where a hypothesis fails the theorem makes no prediction, and the measured contrast change there is not systematically different in sign, which suggests the conditions are sufficient rather than necessary. We state the failures rather than exclude them. For the safety layer we report how often each of the three constraints fails and which one binds. Boundary sharpness is not worsened on 104 of the 173 images, reported as a count and not a mean because the per image worst case is what matters for trusting an individual scan. Of the three constraints, the energy constraint and the bounded change constraint hold on all 173 images and only the no sacrifice constraint ever fails, on 38 of them, so it is the binding one. Acceptance needs two of three and no image falls below two, so the layer returns the candidate in full on every test image. We say in the paper that it is therefore a guard whose bound was measured rather than a mechanism shown to intervene. The allocation map itself is also reported, its mean, spread, minimum and maximum, and the fraction of pixels at either clamp, which is zero by construction after the repair. The map spans 0.556 to 0.793 with mean 0.726 and standard deviation 0.050, and 0.00 percent of pixels sit at either end of the clamp, against every pixel of every image before the repair.
changes: Section V I is new.
Section I B and Section IV C point forward to it.
The macros are generated from outputs/revision/diagnostics_nafnet.json by revision/make_tables.py.

Comment 3.16.response: We agree and we have added the comparison. Our object is a correction layer attached to a frozen denoiser, so a fair competitor has to act on the same input rather than replace the denoiser. We compare in two directions. Across backbones of matched size. The four backbones are all scaled to about seven million parameters and trained on the same split with the same schedule, so the wrapper is added to four comparable denoisers rather than to one convenient one. Against post correction of matched complexity, which is what we read the comment to ask. Section V G adds three competitors that all read the same frozen backbone output. The first is a corrector of the same size trained with the same objective, the same warm start and the same ten epochs, but with the rule layer replaced by a uniform allocation for the whole of training. It was trained before the gate search that produced the selected models, so it uses the percentile gate and the earlier dead zone rather than the tissue bounded gate NAFNet was finally selected with, and we say so rather than claiming a match we cannot verify. We narrowed the text to match the code rather than leaving the mismatch. Section V G now says that this competitor is the same architecture with the same parameter budget and the same objective, trained for the same ten epochs, with the rule layer replaced by a uniform allocation for the whole of training rather than only at test time. It was fitted before the gate search, so it carries the percentile gate and not the tissue bounded gate NAFNet was selected with, which makes it matched in architecture and not in configuration. The paper says so, and the row is labeled uniform allocation, trained. The second and third are classical operators, unsharp masking and contrast limited adaptive histogram equalization, with their strength tuned on the forty image validation subset under the same rule used for our own constants. The lower block of Table 5 reports all of them. Training with a uniform allocation reaches plus 4.11 percent contrast and plus 11.58 percent tissue contrast index against plus 3.71 and plus 2.42 for the full method, and it pays 0.42 dB of fidelity against 0.17 dB. It is worse on the other four, at 0.71 against 1.21 percent on edge preservation, 3.83 against 4.16 on boundary sharpness, 16.2 against 23.3 on the speckle measure and 5.8 against 10.7 on the signal to noise ratio, so the two are not ordered. The two classical operators reach the largest tissue contrast index in the table by a wide margin, plus 39.5 and plus 53.0 against plus 2.4, while on contrast only adaptive equalization exceeds the wrapper, at plus 6.5 against plus 3.7, and unsharp masking falls well below it at plus 0.6. Both fail on everything else, lowering edge preservation by about 3.5 percent, raising boundary sharpness by about 25 percent by sharpening noise along with structure, and lowering the speckle measure by about 36 percent, with adaptive equalization also costing 4.4 dB. We state in the paper that the comparison does not show the rule layer produces the largest clinical numbers, only that the alternatives which produce larger numbers change the image several times as much and without a per pixel account of why.

Comment 3.17.response: This question and Reviewer 1 comment 4 are the reason we found the defect described at the start of this letter, so we answer plainly. In the submitted version the constants of the fuzzy layer were the initial values of learnable parameters that never moved, because the layer was saturated and received no gradient. The honest answer to how they were computed is that they were not. In the revised version every constant is listed with its origin in Section V B of the main paper. The budgets are fixed by the identity stated in Section III C rather than chosen, and their relative sizes preserve the ordering of the submitted version so the rule that dominated still dominates. The rule weights and the base level are learned. Section V B states that exactly one quantity of the objective was tuned, the fidelity dead zone, together with the choice of background rule, and that both were selected on the validation split at three seeds by a recorded rule. We also found that ten weight flags in the training script are parsed and never used, so the four settings of the earlier search differed in the dead zone alone. Section V B now names all ten and the weights that do reach the loss are printed in Equations 14 to 19. The release documents that. Section V F reports the sensitivity study. No variation of any constant turns any of the six clinical measures negative. Over the fourteen variations the contrast gain lies between 3.5 and 4.5 percent and the fidelity cost between 0.16 and 0.23 dB, and replacing the Lukasiewicz conjunction by the product or by the minimum moves the contrast gain from 3.7 to 3.5 percent.

Comment 3.18.response: The reviewer is right that adapting the confidence head is training and that its cost should be stated. Section V K is new and reports, for each backbone, the size of the head, the data used to fit it, the number of epochs, the wall clock time, and the spread across the three seeds. The wrapper adds 168630 parameters shared across backbones plus a head whose size follows the width of the feature tensor it reads, 4659 for KBNet, 7263 for NAFNet, 85908 for SwinIR and 234273 for DnCNN. The trainable totals are therefore 173289, 175893, 254538 and 402903, so KBNet is below NAFNet and DnCNN is above SwinIR rather than both lying between them, which an earlier draft of this answer had wrong. The frozen backbones they are measured against are 7583521, 7009881, 6939289 and 7029013 parameters, giving 2.3, 2.5, 3.7 and 5.7 percent. Every backbone is fitted on the same 1388 PKU37 pairs for the same ten epochs from the same warm start, so only the wall clock and the seed spread vary. Fitting one seed takes 2.0 minutes for NAFNet, 2.5 for KBNet, 3.9 for DnCNN and 8.3 for SwinIR on one RTX 5070 Ti, an ordering set by the cost of one backbone forward pass. The fidelity spread across the three seeds is 0.02 dB for NAFNet, 0.06 for SwinIR, 0.08 for KBNet and 0.21 for DnCNN. We also separate two claims that the submitted paper mixed. What transfers with no training at all is the whole wrapper applied to another scanner, Table 4. What needs training is the move to a new backbone, because the head reads that backbone's features, and that cost is what Section V K reports. The tissue contrast index of DnCNN has mean plus 0.99 percent with a seed to seed standard deviation of 1.62, and the edge preservation of KBNet has mean 0.00 percent with a standard deviation of 0.07, both sample standard deviations over the three seeds as used everywhere in the paper. Both are visible in Table 3, where bold marks a mean that exceeds its spread and neither cell is bold, and Section V D names them in the text.
